Game two at Oliver's, October 20th, 2026, same four-person pod (me, Oliver, Tom, Ryan): Shabraz and Brallin, the Sharknado deck. Shabraz wheels went pretty well. I mulliganed. I don't even know if I should have held the hand that I had, because I only had one playable creature in it and a bunch of wheels. That's part of my pilot's feedback: it feels like there might be too many wheels in the wheel deck. Two commanders is two commander taxes on the board; Brallin is red, he's a four drop. Making people discard their hand is not something people enjoy. From a political standpoint, if the whole deck is premised around constantly making you discard your hand and draw a new one (granted, Oliver is making people discard creatures on the board and all this other stuff) there is something annoying about it: you're trying to play the game, you've got cards in hand, you're setting stuff up, and somebody constantly makes you discard. The wheels need to be few and far between; they need to come in and hit when Brallin or Shabraz are on the table. Those should be finisher kind of things: Shabraz and Brallin are already out, they're kind of big, and I drop a wheel on them, discard seven, discard four, boom boom boom, Brallin, everybody takes four, then everybody draws maybe seven, I gain seven life, Shabraz gets seven bigger, then into another one, make them real big, tap a red, give him trample, flying trample big commander shark coming at you. So it does feel like this is actually good, but there's some calibration that needs to go into that deck specifically: I think there's too many wheels. It's also a good reminder that you've got to really downweight those goldfish metrics, because not factoring in removal and opponent interactions and things like that just moves the deck in the wrong direction.

## Game 1: Sharknado (loss)

The engine ran well and the sequencing felt right. Alex's warp deck was a faster class of deck, and a land-heavy opener without payoffs never found the wheels.

**Table:** Sean on Sharknado, Alex on his warp deck, Ryan on Slivers (nothing much popped off for Ryan).

**What worked**

- Draw/discard loops moved Sean through the deck all game. Pieces in play: the Ledger card (connive: draw, discard) and Bonnie/Annie (haste, draw a card, discard a card).
- Smothering Tithe produced steady Treasure. That was the ramp the hand needed, and it may have been under-used.
- Sean cast a lot of spells. Alex looked at the board and said things were happening.
- Deflecting Swat was in hand this game too.

**What didn't**

- No wheel drawn. Sean held the commanders back to avoid a wipe and wait for a wheel that never showed.
- Kept a hand with a lot of lands, ramp, one artifact dork and one wheel, but few creatures or payoffs. Gemstone Caverns was in the opener, but Sean rolled highest and went first, so he never got the luck-counter version for any-color mana.
- Open question: kept hand or mulligan? Sean now thinks the mulligan call was not ideal.
- Commander tension: wants both commanders out, with no clean way to cheat them out or ramp faster. Discard-a-card effects also slow the deck; a discard-to-top-of-library option was considered but costs tempo.

**Alex's warp deck**

- Ramps to about 15 mana and warps out a large number of creatures.
- An artifact lets him end the turn before his end step, so the warped creatures stay on the battlefield. Big threats arrive cheaply and keep coming.
- Sean's read: without Alex's warp turns, Sharknado does much more. Open question: how to beat this deck.

Lesson: | Sharknado | Opener had lands and ramp but no payoffs; the mulligan call is in question. Holding commanders for a wheel cost tempo when no wheel came. | Find a way to cheat out or ramp into both commanders sooner. Look at wheel count and the discard-a-card drag. |
Lesson: | Sharknado vs. Alex's warp deck | Warp turns outpace Sharknado. | Work out an answer to the warp deck. |

Pilot's Log — Nov 3, 2026, Oliver's 5-Player Pod

Session summary
Record 1–1. Heliod won game 1 on Approach of the Second Sun; Sharknado lost game 2 to Ryan's T'Vol going infinite around turn 8–9. First five-player pod in a while, and the table stepped up to bracket 4.

Table, game 2: Sean, Shabraz + Brallin, Sharknado (loss). Ryan, T'Vol (WIN, infinite combo).

Sharknado assembled every multiplier and 36 Treasure but never saw a wheel. Second straight log with the same note: payoffs lag the engine.

Game 2 — Sharknado, Shabraz + Brallin (LOSS to Ryan's T'Vol)
Lost with lethal fully assembled except for the one card type that triggers it. Ryan went infinite with T'Vol around turn 8–9 before it came around again.
Board at the end
Shabraz — On board
Brallin — On board (trample source)
Fiery Emancipation — On board (triple damage)
Smothering Tithe — On board; 36 Treasure banked
Mystic Remora — On board, drawing 2 per trigger
Teferi's Ageless Insight — On board
Tutor — In hand, aimed at Shark Typhoon
Wheel (Windfall or similar) — Never drawn
The planned line: tutor Shark Typhoon, cycle it with the Treasure for a ~34-power flying shark, give it trample via Brallin, triple the damage with Fiery Emancipation. One wheel would have closed it from any seat.
What the pilot did about it
• Dug 9–10 cards off Remora and Teferi looking for any wheel, ideally an instant-speed one to fire on another player's turn. None.
• Kept the deck alive through several wraths and wipes; piloting on the defensive side was fine.
• After the game, flipped through the remaining library to see where the first wheel sat. It was deep.
Deck read, one game's evidence
• Sequencing gap persists after the last refactor. The engine (Tithe, Remora, Treasure) comes online reliably; the payoff (a wheel) does not.
• Embercleave keeps appearing early and getting discarded to the loot engine. Equipment and artifact multipliers may be too slow for the deck's tempo, or there are too many multipliers per wheel.
• The forced-discard half of the draw engine is sometimes a cost, not a benefit. Modal draw (discard optional) would fit the hand better.
• Pilot is explicitly cautious about changing the list on one data point. About a third of the deck is still proxies; he's holding off on buying until the list feels final.

Follow-ups for the workbench
Sharknado gets the research; Heliod gets a pilot's-manual note. No list changes yet.
Sharknado — research requests
[ ] Wheel-count audit: how many wheels are in the current list, at what mana values, and the expected turn of the first wheel given the draw engine. Compare against when the engine pieces (Tithe, Remora, commanders) typically land.
[ ] Tutor lines for wheels: which tutors in the list can find a wheel, and a short "what to tutor for when" map (board has multipliers but no wheel; board has a wheel but no commander; etc.).
[ ] Repeatable wheels ("wheels on legs"): creature, artifact, and enchantment wheels that stay on board, so one draw turns into every turn.
[ ] Modal draw: effects that draw without forced discard, or where the discard is optional, to replace some of the loot pieces.
[ ] Equipment and multiplier density: is Embercleave (and similar) earning its slot at this deck's tempo, and are there more multipliers than wheels to feed them?
[ ] Hold all of the above as hypotheses until two or three more games are logged. Pilot does not want a swap off one game.
Purchase decision
• Roughly a third of Sharknado is proxies. Buying waits on the research above and a couple more logged games.

Pilot's Notes — Tue Nov 10, 2026, Oliver's house
Pod: Sean, Oliver, Tom, Ryan (4-player). Bracket: 3. Record on the night: 0–3. Decks piloted: Goblin Storm (Zada) ×2, Shabraz, the Sky Shark ×1.

Table context
• Tom: Purphoros (mono-red ETB pings). Oliver: Balin (token maker; Krenko in game 3). Ryan: Tiny Bones (shared graveyard / steal).
• Pre-game talk was precons / bracket 2. Sean has no bracket 2 deck, so brought his lowest-power bracket 3 (Goblin Storm). Opponents' bracket 3 decks are highly optimized and aim to win around turn four.
• Games were very fast: game 1 ran about 30 minutes.

Game 3 — Shabraz, the Sky Shark (loss, Oliver on Krenko)
What happened
• Deck was recently optimized to focus solely on drawing cards and buffing the shark.
• Oliver landed Krenko. Table asked Sean to remove it. Sean held Swords to Plowshares and a second two-mana removal spell and did not use either, prioritizing momentum and getting Shabraz down.
• After Shabraz resolved, Sean had a further turn with open mana and still did not remove Krenko.
• Oliver went off; Sean took 30-plus damage in one turn. Game over.
Assessment
• 100% piloting error. Had removal, had mana, had a full turn, had the table's read. Cards in hand would have made Shabraz very large.
• No deck changes. Right hand, misplayed. Needs more reps — track Shabraz across more games before any tuning review.

Cross-game piloting lessons
• Threat removal beats tempo. Same pattern as Sep 2026 notes (Ur Dragon telegraphing, Edgar leaving Elspeth exposed): preferring own momentum over removing the obvious table threat. Rule: when the whole table names the threat and only you can answer it, answer it.
• Kill-on-sight list: Purphoros (Tom), Krenko (Oliver).
• Deny the Sol Ring opener. Early artifact removal is a legitimate tempo play against this pod; expect salt, do it anyway.
• Enchantment removal should be a standing slot audit across decks.
• Tier context: Oliver/Tom table bracket 3 ≈ optimized, turn-four clock; B-team (Steven, Stuart, David) bracket 3 ≈ turn 6–7 clock.

Pod night, Thursday November 12, 2026, at Steven's house. Four-player pod, two games; the other three played the same deck both games. Steven: Magda, mono red (cheap dwarves make treasure, tutors an artifact or dragon onto the battlefield, always fetches Utvara Hellkite, pops off fast). David: Golem partner-commander deck (slow, still being built). Stuart: Rotcleaver zombie typal (zombies come back, decayed tokens, Blood Artist and Zulaport Cutthroat sacrifice drain).

Game 2: Shabraz and Brallin (loss). Sean died at 1 life, one turn before a Wheel of Fortune comeback. He is happy with how the deck worked and how it piloted.
Early game. Mulliganed once. Kept the second hand: more land, but no small creatures and no blockers. Missed a land drop. No creature until about turn four. With no creatures for four turns, everybody attacked Sean. Having taken the last win did not help. Short on mana for Shabraz, he cast Brallin instead. Brallin costs four, one less.
The key turn. 1. Smothering Tithe was out, with Brallin as a blocker. 2. Sean activated the wheel on legs: pay one blue and tap, everybody discards their hand and draws equal to the most cards discarded (heard as "Essence Valdarin"). 3. Brallin triggered: +1/+1 counters and damage across the table. 4. Everyone drew about five. Tithe made 14 treasure; it would have been 15, but Steven paid two for one draw. 5. Faerie Mastermind kept everybody drawing. 6. With the mana, Shabraz came out. Sean started wheeling and Shabraz got very big.
Decision points. Kept a land-heavy hand with no early creatures: no board until turn four, took everyone's attacks (flagged as an observation). Cast Brallin when short of Shabraz mana: a body on defense, and the discard cards in hand still worked with him; nice to have Brallin as the fallback; he is not the main win line anymore, but the discard engine is still there. Swung Brallin at Steven: Steven blocked with two creatures, Sean killed one of his dragons; not sure whether this was a mistake. Swung Shabraz at Steven, 18 flying, trample, commander damage: Steven blocked with two 6/6 dragons, 6 commander damage got through; great, removed the big evasive bodies that are core to Steven's engine. Held the treasure instead of casting the humans in hand: Steven swung back, Sean sacrificed Esper Sentinel and another human and blocked with Brallin, left at 1 life; should have spent it, humans can be given flying, and he needed them as blockers on a wide board. Left Stuart's Blood Artist on the table: every creature death drained the table and gained Stuart life; if Blood Artist comes out, remove it early.
What worked. Shabraz gives the humans flying and Brallin gives the shark trample. With spare treasure Sean could pick either: evasion on attack, or tap a mana to give a human flying and block.
How it ended. Sean was at 1 life with Shabraz out and Wheel of Fortune in hand. His plan: wheel everybody, buff Shabraz, get his life back up to 8, then use the new cards and the treasure to come back. On Stuart's end step, Stuart sacrificed a zombie and dealt 1 damage. Sean died before his turn. Steven died after that. Stuart took the win. David pieced things together around turn eight or nine, way too late against a deck like Magda.
Sean's closing read: Shabraz did its thing, was a real threat, and did a ton of damage to Steven. He is unsure whether he got outraced. A pretty good game. Open question from Sean: was swinging Brallin at Steven a mistake?
Sean, the next day: "Shabraz did great work and worked the table, hurt Stephen alot (didn't aim at Stuart or David) but I like what it did!!!! Overall, great night!"
